implementation_notes: The JavaScript engines (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore) inline automatically and aggressively at hot call sites, and again the lever is shape rather than annotation. A monomorphic property access and a small method inline; a megamorphic property access (an object with many different hidden classes at the same site) defeats inline caches, and this - not call overhead - is the dominant JavaScript performance cliff. The standard fix is shape stability: create objects the same way every time (same property order, same hidden class), avoid polymorphic call sites, and avoid megamorphic dictionary-mode objects. There is no inline keyword, and V8's TurboFan will deoptimise a function whose shape assumptions change (adding a property after creation deoptimises it). Manual inlining by copying a body into a hot loop is sometimes done but removes the function's identity and its ability to be optimised as a unit.
idiom_name: automatic JIT inlining and inline caches; shape stability (monomorphic sites) is the real lever; no inline keyword
pitfalls: No inline keyword exists; the lever is making the call site monomorphic and the object's hidden class stable.
Adding a property to an object after creation changes its shape and deoptimises the functions that touched it - build objects complete.
A megamorphic call site (many hidden classes at one site) defeats the inline cache; this is the dominant JS perf cliff and it is invisible without an IC-aware profile.
Copying a function body manually to avoid a 'call' removes its identity and prevents the JIT from optimising it as a unit; fix the shape instead.
Inlining happens in the optimised tier, so a micro-benchmark of a hot function differs from a one-shot call - measure in a steady-state loop.
